text:
Ayoub c. Canada (Attorney
General)

2005 QCCA 1228

COURT OF
APPEAL

CANADA

PROVINCE
OF QUEBEC

REGISTRY
OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-10-003335-054

(500-36-003818-054)

DATE:

DECEMBER
13, 2005

PRESENT
:

THE HONOURABLE

ALLAN R. HILTON, J.A.

AHMED
AYOUB

APPELLANT
– Petitioner

v.

THE
ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA

ON
BEHALF OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

RESPONDENT
– Respondent

JUDGMENT

[
1
]

Ahmed Ayoub seeks his judicial interim release
pursuant to section 20 of the
Extradition Act
(the Act)
[1]

following the issuance of an order of committal into custody by a judge of the
Superior Court under section 29 of the Act and his appeal of that
committal to this Court. The Attorney General of Canada contests the
application, but the parties have agreed on conditions of release should I be
of the view that Mr. Ayoub's release should be ordered pending the
determination of his appeal.

[
2
]

Mr. Ayoub stands accused of sexual assault
in the Circuit Court of the Sixth Judicial Circuit of the State of Florida in
and for Pinellas County. The events giving rise to the accusation are multiple
assaults on a 14‑year old girl that are said to have occurred between
March 22 and March 26, 2003 at a retirement centre in Clearwater
where both Mr. Ayoub and the alleged victim were employed.

[
3
]

Mr. Ayoub says he was born in Palestine in
1967, but at the relevant time of the events in issue, he enjoyed permanent
resident status in the United States. Other members of his immediate family
were also resident in Florida.

[
4
]

According to the record and to what I was
informed at the hearing before me by counsel, Mr. Ayoub arrived by bus in
Canada in early April of 2003. He was authorized to enter Canada as a visitor.
After his arrival, however, he initiated a claim for refugee status. Broadly
speaking, he contends that the atmosphere in the United States has been
continuously deteriorating for persons of Arab origin since September 11,
2001, and that he fears for his life and security if he were to return to
Palestine because of his political views and his recent conversion to
Christianity.

[
5
]

In other words, Mr. Ayoub asserts that his
presence in Canada as of early April 2003 is unrelated to the events that are
the subject of the charges against him that are alleged to have been committed in
the latter part of March of the same year.

[
6
]

After his arrival in Canada, Mr. Ayoub did
have some contact with police authorities in Florida in the middle part of
April of 2003, at which time he indicated he would be going back to Florida
shortly and that he would call the investigating police officer upon his
return. Instead, Mr. Ayoub remained in Montreal, and then filed his claim
for refugee status. In December of 2003, the investigating officer in Florida
contacted a sergeant–detective with the Montreal police, and asked for his
assistance in locating Mr. Ayoub.

[
7
]

Since arriving in Canada, Mr. Ayoub
secured a position as an auxiliary nurse at the Jewish General Hospital. In
June of this year, the State of Florida formally requested the extradition of
Mr. Ayoub for prosecution. Mr. Ayoub was arrested at his home on
October 19 under the authority of a warrant issued by a judge of the Superior
Court following an application to that effect by the Attorney General of Canada
in virtue of section 16 of the Act.

[
8
]

Shortly thereafter, Mr. Ayoub presented a
motion to the Superior Court for his judicial interim release pursuant to sub‑section 18(1)(b)
and section 19 of the Act, which, amongst other provisions, makes sub‑
section 515(10)

of the
Criminal Code
applicable in the circumstances. Under the latter
sub‑section, an accused's detention can only be justified on one of the
following grounds:

(a)
where the detention is necessary to ensure his or her attendance in court in
order to be dealt with according to law;

(b) where
the detention is necessary for the protection or safety of the public,
including any victim of or witness to the offence, having regard to all the
circumstances including any substantial likelihood that the accused will, if
released from custody, commit a criminal offence or interfere with the
administration of justice; and

(c) on
any other just cause being shown and, without limiting the generality of the
foregoing, where the detention is necessary in order to maintain confidence in
the administration of justice, having regard to all the circumstances,
including the apparent strength of the prosecution's case, the gravity of the
nature of the offence, the circumstances surrounding its commission and the
potential for a lengthy term of imprisonment.

[
9
]

The Attorney General of Canada relied on either
of sub‑sections (a) and (c) to oppose Mr. Ayoub's
application.

[
10
]

The judge of the Superior Court before whom the
application was presented on November 10, Mongeau, J., observed that
Mr. Ayoub carried the burden of proof to demonstrate on a balance of
probabilities that none of the foregoing criteria were established. He also
noted the applicability of sub‑
section 11(e)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms

"not to be denied reasonable bail
without just cause" to a person whose extradition was sought by a foreign
state, and he took account of the fact that the extradition hearing was to take
place not long after on November 22.

[
11
]

Insofar as relevant, Mongeau, J. summarized
the evidence before him in the following manner:

[19]      Le
requérant fait valoir qu'il est maintenant bien établi au Canada et qu'il
occupe un emploi rémunéré comme infirmier auxiliaire à Montréal depuis le mois
d'août 2003.  La preuve révèle de plus que son passeport est entre les mains
des autorités canadiennes de l'immigration puisque le requérant a fait une
demande d'asile au Canada.  Le requérant réside maintenant au […] à Montréal.
Il fréquente sérieusement une amie, madame Rita Dallanian, depuis une année.
Il assure le Tribunal qu'il sera présent à la Cour aux moments requis.

[20]      L'agent
d'audience Jean-Denis St‑Pierre, de l'Agence des services frontaliers du
Canada (autrefois Immigration Canada), témoigne que tous les aspects du dossier
du requérant sont suspendus dans l'attente de la disposition de la Requête en
extradition.

[21]      Madame
Dallanian témoigne qu'elle est prête à se porter garante financièrement pour
assurer la présence du requérant devant la Cour.  Elle se dit prête à déposer
une somme en argent liquide de 3 000 $ et, s'il le fallait, à
hypothéquer un immeuble dont elle est propriétaire et dont l'équité se situe
aux environs de cent mille dollars.

[22]      Madame
Dallanian est directrice commerciale dans une institution bancaire à Montréal.

[23]      Elle
témoigne qu'il est de son intention de vivre éventuellement avec le requérant
dans les semaines qui suivront sa remise en liberté.  Elle indique que le
requérant s'entend bien avec son fils de 12 ans.  Son fils le considère
comme un père.  Le requérant aurait un effet positif sur lui. Ses notes
scolaires sont à la hausse.  Le père biologique de l'enfant est absent depuis
neuf années.

[24]      Madame
Dallanian dit qu'elle est au courant de certains détails des faits et gestes
reprochés au requérant mais qu'elle ne pose pas de questions à ce sujet, se
contentant d'accepter ce que le requérant lui dit sur sa non implication dans
ces événements.

[25]      Le
requérant témoigne qu'il a collaboré avec les policiers qui sont entrés en
communication avec lui.  Il a accepté la suggestion du sergent-détective
Paradiso du SPVM de passer un polygraphe.  Il a de plus rappelé l'officier de
police de la ville de Clearwater qui tentait de le rejoindre par l'entremise de
l'un de ses frères.

[26]      Pour
sa part, l'intimé soumet qu'il est nécessaire de détenir le requérant pour
assurer sa présence devant le tribunal le 22 novembre prochain.

[27]
L'intimé soulève notamment que le requérant s'est enfui de l'état de la Floride
quelques jours seulement après que les présumés actes et gestes qui lui sont
reprochés aient été commis.

[28]      L'intimé
soumet également que la preuve révèle que le requérant n'aurait pas indiqué aux
autorités de l'Immigration canadienne sa véritable date d'entrée au Canada et
qu'il aurait décidé de demander le statut de réfugié le 16 avril 2003 le jour
après avoir su que les policiers de la Floride le recherchaient et voulaient
lui parler.

[29]      De
plus, l'intimé indique que la preuve révèle que le requérant aurait appelé son
employeur en Floride le 2 avril 2003 prétendant être en Caroline du Nord tandis
que l'afficheur du téléphone indiquait un appel provenant du code régional 514.

[30]      Le
requérant témoigne qu'il a quitté la Floride le 4 avril 2003 parce que
depuis le mois de septembre 2001, la situation aux États‑Unis pour les
arabes n'était pas facile et que sa qualité de vie ne cessait de s'aggraver.

[31]      Il
vaut de rappeler que le requérant nie catégoriquement avoir posé les gestes
qu'on lui reproche.

[32]      Deux
de ses frères sont toujours résidents de l'état de la Floride à Clearwater, là,
doit-on le rappeler, où le requérant résidait avant son départ pour le Canada.

[33]      Le
requérant témoigne que sa relation avec ses frères n'est pas très bonne depuis
qu'il s'est converti au christianisme.

[
12
]

Mongeau, J. concluded that Mr. Ayoub's
application should be dismissed. His analysis of the evidence and the
applicable principles of law are set out in the paragraphs that follow.

[37]      En
premier lieu, la question se pose si le requérant risque de tenter de fuir la
justice s'il est mis en liberté provisoire.

[38]      Le
Tribunal estime que les gestes posés antérieurement par le requérant lorsqu'il
a quitté précipitamment la Floride peu de jours après les événements reprochés,
sa demande de statut de réfugié non pas dès son arrivée au Canada qu'il situe
lui-même au 6 avril 2003 mais le 16 avril 2003, soit le lendemain d'une
conversation téléphonique qu'il tient avec un officier enquêteur de la police
de Clearwater ainsi que sa crainte très élevée d'être retourné dans son pays
d'origine par les États-Unis laissent un doute sérieux quant à sa présence
devant la Cour lorsqu'il sera question de son extradition aux États-Unis.
Cette audition aura lieu le 22 novembre prochain.

[39]      Le
requérant n'a pu convaincre le Tribunal selon la norme de preuve requise que sa
mise en liberté provisoire n'est pas nécessaire pour assurer sa présence devant
la Cour.

[40]      Certes,
son amie, madame Dallanian pourrait répondre financièrement pour lui afin
d'assurer cette présence.  Par contre, le Tribunal n'est pas satisfait que les
liens entre cette dernière et le requérant sont assez solides pour annihiler
ses craintes à ce sujet.

[41]      Il
vaut de dire qu'avant son arrestation le 19 octobre 2005, le requérant ne
partageait pas entièrement sa vie avec madame Dallanian.  Tous les deux
habitaient à des endroits différents.

[42]      Interrogé
sur sa relation avec cette dernière, le requérant répond qu'elle est sa
"girlfriend".

[43]      Madame
Dallanian témoigne qu'avant l'arrestation du requérant c'était qu'une question
de semaines pour que les deux vivent sous le même toit.

[44]      Le
Tribunal estime que cette preuve n'est pas présentée de façon prépondérante.

[45]      Le
témoignage du requérant ne laisse pas suffisamment de raisons qui permettent de
croire que ces deux personnes s'apprêtaient à faire vie commune, c'est-à-dire à
établir une relation sur une base plus solide, plus permanente.

[46]      Le
Tribunal ne peut donc retenir cet aspect de la preuve et s'en servir le cas
échéant pour se convaincre de la solidité de l'attachement du requérant envers
madame Dallanian et son fils, ce qui aurait pu être un élément important dans
l'évaluation que doit faire le Tribunal à savoir si le requérant a démontré à
sa satisfaction que sa détention était ou non justifiée dans les circonstances
pour assurer sa présence devant la Cour lorsque requise.

[47]      Le
Tribunal a également considéré que le requérant semble toujours avoir un emploi
rémunéré stable à Montréal comme infirmier auxiliaire.

[48]      Certes,
il s'agit là d'un lien pouvant aider à assurer sa présence devant la Cour lorsque
requis.

[49]
Par contre, la preuve révèle qu'en quittant précipitamment la Floride, le
requérant a laissé en plan un emploi d'infirmier sans prévenir ses employeurs
préalablement à son départ.

[50]      Après
analyse de l'ensemble de la preuve, le Tribunal estime que la détention du
requérant jusqu'à l'audition de la requête en extradition est justifiée dans
les circonstances.

[51]      Il
n'est donc pas nécessaire de rendre une décision sur l'alinéa c) de
l'
article 515(10)
du
Code criminel
.

[
13
]

I should mention for the sake of clarity that
the present matter is a fresh application by Mr. Ayoub and not an appeal
from the judgment of Mongeau, J. Nevertheless, as appears from the
extracts I have quoted, Mongeau, J. heard
viva voce
evidence as
well as examining the various documents that have been made available to me. In
this application, Mr. Ayoub at no time challenged the accuracy of any of
those findings, although of course he draws different conclusions from them.

[
14
]

It is also important to record the following new
facts that have occurred since the judgment of Mongeau, J.:

•

an order of committal was entered by a judge of
the Superior Court on November 22, and the minutes of the hearing state that
"the accused admits that there is a prima facie case";

•

Mr. Ayoub has appealed that committal, and
invokes in particular the unconstitutional nature of sections 32 and 33 of the
Act as being inconsistent with
section 7
of the
Canadian Charter
;
[2]

•

the relationship of Mr. Ayoub and
Ms. Dalalian has been rendered more definitive and they have mandated a
notary to take steps to establish a civil union between them as of January 4,
2006;
[3]

•

Mr. Ayoub has moved all of his furniture to
the residence of Ms. Dalalian, and he has given formal notice of his
change of address to that of her residence.

[
15
]

Section 20 of the Act renders

section 679
of the
Criminal Code
applicable to a hearing such as
this one. In order to succeed, Mr. Ayoub must establish on a balance of
probabilities all of the following criteria set out in sub‑section
679(3):

(a)  the appeal or
application for leave to appeal is not frivolous;

(b)  he will surrender
himself into custody in accordance with the terms of the order; and

(c)  his detention is not
necessary in the public interest.

[
16
]

The Attorney General concedes that Mr. Ayoub's appeal is not
frivolous, although his counsel argues that it is weak in light of what is
really in issue in
Ferras
,
[4]

and that a contextual approach to the concept of "public interest"
without the need to consider it impermissibly vague
[5]
leads to the conclusion that his
detention would not be necessary for that reason either. Rather, the debate
before me focuses on the second criterion, that is, whether Mr. Ayoub
would surrender himself into custody in the event of the dismissal of his
appeal.

[
17
]

Counsel on behalf of Mr. Ayoub argues
forcefully that whatever uncertainty that Mongeau, J. may have entertained
as to the durability of the relationship between him and Ms. Dalalian
[6]

has now been dissipated by their firm intention to establish a civil union,
that he has given notice of a change of address to her residence and that he
has caused all of his furniture to be moved there as well. It is further argued
that Mr. Ayoub does not constitute a flight risk in light of his pending
claim for refugee status in Canada since there is no other country to which he
can go inasmuch as his travel documents are in the hands of Canadian
authorities, his status as a permanent resident in the United States is no
longer available to him as he has lived outside that country for an extended
period of time, and he would not wish to return to Palestine because of his
political views and his recent conversion to Christianity.

[
18
]

I am satisfied that the steps taken by
Mr. Ayoub and Ms. Dalalian to render their relationship a permanent one
removes one of the concerns expressed by Mongeau, J. Nevertheless, the
circumstances of Mr. Ayoub's precipitous departure from the United States
and the fact that he did not apply immediately upon arrival in Canada for
refugee status are consistent with a reasonable apprehension that he would not
surrender himself into custody in the event of an adverse judgment on his
appeal against the issuance of the warrant of committal.

[
19
]

None of the facts that that have occurred since
the judgment of Mongeau, J. alleviate the serious concerns mentioned in
paragraphs [38] and [49] of his judgment relative to Mr. Ayoub's
conduct both prior to and subsequent to his arrival in Canada.
[7]

Moreover, being in Montreal would not preclude him from avoiding surrender by
going elsewhere in Canada even if his capacity to travel outside Canada and
gain legal admittance to another country is severely impaired. Finally in this
respect, if Mongeau, J. was of the view that Mr. Ayoub could not be
trusted to attend his committal hearing that was to take place a mere
12 days after the hearing before him, I cannot ignore that if I was to
grant his application, Mr. Ayoub would be at liberty for a lengthy period
of time given the other steps that have to be accomplished under the Act for
the extradition process to be completed and the availability of judicial
recourses against a potentially adverse ministerial decision.

[
20
]

In any event, the underlying basis for
Mr. Ayoub's stated reasons for coming to Canada remain imprecise and thus
they are unpersuasive.

[
21
]

It is not enough simply to assert in a general
way that persons such as Mr. Ayoub are subject to "harassment
problems directed towards the Arab people" in the United States since
September 11, 2001 without even a single illustration of any such
harassment, much less one directed at him. It is equally insufficient for
Mr. Ayoub to merely state, without any supporting explanation, that he
fears for his life if he returns to Palestine because of his conversion to
Christianity.

[
22
]

It would require a considerable degree of
naivety to accept Mr. Ayoub's submissions and to give effect to them by
authorizing his judicial interim release. To do so, I would have to disregard
the proximity of his abrupt departure from his home, family and job in Florida
(early April of 2003) to the dates of occurrence of the alleged events for
which he is charged (March 22 to 26 of 2003), and his subsequent
arrival here as a visitor, after which he applied for refugee status only when
he became aware that police authorities in Florida were anxious to speak to
him.

[
23
]

I therefore conclude that Mr. Ayoub has not
satisfied all of the criteria of sub‑
section 679(3)
of the
Criminal
Code
. Accordingly, his application for judicial interim release is
dismissed.

ALLAN R.
HILTON, J.A.

Mtre Clemente Monterosso

For the petitioner

Mtre Sabrina Delli Fraine

For
the respondent

Date
of hearing:

December
1, 2005

These sections, which deal with the rules of evidence at an
extradition hearing such as the one at which Mr. Ayoub was committed, are
under review by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of
Ferras
v.
United
States of America et al.
, docket number 30211, in which judgment was
reserved on October 17, 2005. In
Ferras
, the person whose extradition is sought is a Canadian
citizen who was indicted in the United States on charges of securities fraud, conspiracy and money laundering. In
the Supreme Court of Canada, Ferras conceded that the extradition judge who
ordered his committal was bound by the Ontario Court of Appeal judgment in
United
States of America
v.
Yang
, (2001),
2001 CanLII 20937 (ON CA)
, 56 O.R. (3d) 52 that
held the impugned provisions of the
Extradition Act
to be
constitutionally valid. He argues, however, that the application of these
provisions to a Canadian citizen offends
sections 6
and
7
of the
Canadian
Charter
.
